name: tinyfft
workload: In-place power-of-two complex double FFT (AVX variant) at lengths 2^17 to 2^20; the README gives no further workload detail.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Empirically, for vectors of length between 2^17 and 2^20, Tiny FFT is faster than FFTW3 with FFTW_MEASURE. For other cases, Tiny FFT is slower than FFTW3.' No numbers are given anywhere in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: README build lines only: 'clang -O3 example.c tinyfft.c -lm' and 'clang -O3 example.c tinyfft_avx.c -lm -march=native'; the flags used for the FFTW comparison are not stated.
tradeoffs: Tiny code base (tinyfft.c 132 lines, tinyfft_avx.c 342 lines). Power-of-two lengths only, double precision complex only, output left in bit-reversal order (so the transform is meant for convolution-style use, not a drop-in FFTW replacement). The AVX variant uses split real/imaginary arrays and needs -march=native. Slower than FFTW3 outside 2^17-2^20 by the author's own statement.
caveats: No benchmark program, results file, CPU model, compiler version or FFTW version is in the repo (files: example.c, tinyfft.c, tinyfft_avx.c and headers; example.c only exercises a convolution on stdin data). The claim is a qualitative author statement with no numbers, so tier D; it is also narrow (a 4-octave size range) and compares against FFTW_MEASURE rather than FFTW_PATIENT or MKL. Last commit 2018-07-24, single author.

name: heFFTe (Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale)
baseline: Distributed 3-D FFT libraries fftMPI, SWFFT, AccFFT and P3DFFT (FFTW-MPI-class); FFTW is heFFTe's own CPU backend
workload: Distributed-memory 2-D/3-D complex FFTs (e.g. 1024^3 on Summit nodes) with pencil or slab decomposition; the repo's speed3d benchmark reports heFFTe's own GFlops/s per backend.
claimed_speedup: No competitor numbers on any page I could open. The repo benchmarks (speed3d_c2c/r2c/r2r.cpp, convolution.cpp) time heFFTe with a chosen backend (stock, FFTW, MKL, cuFFT, rocFFT, oneMKL) and print 'Performance: <x> GFlops/s'. Paper claims seen only through WebSearch result summaries, not verified: ICCS 2020 paper 'heFFTe: Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale' reports more than 40x speedup of GPU local kernels over CPU state-of-the-art libraries and over 2x for the whole FFT, about 90% of roofline peak at 1024^3 on Summit; a follow-up reportedly shows heFFTe about 2x faster than fftMPI and SWFFT on GPU and up to 2x faster on one node and 1.65x on two nodes than another distributed library.
hardware: Not stated on any opened page; README acknowledges OLCF resources (Summit per the papers).
stars_or_usage: 59 stars; DOE Exascale Computing Project library (ICL UTK / ORNL)
tradeoffs: MPI-based distributed FFT; local 1-D/2-D kernels are delegated to FFTW, MKL, oneMKL, cuFFT or rocFFT backends, so heFFTe is a communication/decomposition layer and does not beat FFTW on a single core. Needs MPI and a backend library; also Fortran and Python bindings. Optional GPU-aware MPI.
caveats: The numbers that matter (papers at icl.utk.edu, iccs-meeting.org, netlib, Springer, arXiv) were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no competitor figures were opened and tier C is a floor: the ICCS 2020 and IPDPS-W 2022 papers are peer-reviewed and a verifier with access may justify tier B (or A if the artifact is public). The headline '40x' compares GPU kernels with CPU kernels, which is hardware not software. The AccFFT GPU runs reportedly failed correctness on Summit. The repo itself contains no head-to-head against other distributed FFT libraries. Docs site (icl-utk-edu.github.io/heffte) is blocked.

name: juFFTe
workload: 1-D/2-D/3-D complex and real FFTs (double precision in the benchmark) on RISC-V RVV 1.0 CPUs; repo fftbench prints time and MFLOPS and, with WITHFFTW=1, FFTW time.
claimed_speedup: Repo README and docs contain no numbers. The accompanying preprint (arXiv 2608.28076, 'Performance Evaluation of Fast Fourier Transforms on Emerging RISC-V Hardware with Vector Extension Support', seen only as a WebSearch snippet because arxiv.org is blocked) says juFFTe 'can yield average performance improvements of up to a factor of three depending on hardware' over FFTW3 on the SiFive X280, the X100 core of the SpacemiT K3 and the C920v2 core of the Sophon SG2044.
compiler_and_flags: Repo defaults in benchmark/Makefile: gfortran -g -O3 -fopenmp; ifx/ifort -g -O3 -qopt-zmm-usage=high -qopenmp; flang -g -O3 plus -ffast-math -mepi; nvfortran -g -O3. Flags used for the paper runs not seen.
hardware: Not stated in the repo. Per the preprint snippet: SiFive X280, SpacemiT K3 (X100 core), Sophon SG2044 (C920v2 core).
tradeoffs: Modern Fortran (2003) library with an FFTW-compatible C/Fortran API (fftw_plan_dft_1d, fftw_execute_dft, fftw_malloc), a C header (src/juffte.h) and OpenMP; link needs the Fortran runtime (-lgfortran) from C/C++. Only RVV kernels are generated so far (Spiral backend; the SVE and plain Spiral options stop at configure time). Inspired by FFTE; FFTE's own license terms were not checked.
caveats: No result tables in the repo; benchmark/sc.sh listed in its README returns 404. The 3x figure is from a preprint abstract (first-party, unreviewed as far as I could see) that I could not open, and the CPU, compiler and flags in it are unverified, so it is tier C; the benchmark code is public, so a verifier with arXiv access could reach tier A if the paper states compiler and flags. Upstream FFTW has no merged RVV kernels as far as I can tell (search results show only an open RVV pull request and issue), so the win may be vectorized code against scalar FFTW rather than an algorithmic win; check how the paper built FFTW. The repo is young (its ten most recent commits are all from September 2026) and benchmark/README.md lists segmentation faults in some environments (raise stack size).

name: PSI-Lib / SpaceTreeLib (P-Orth tree, SPaC-tree; also contains the Pkd-tree)
baseline: Boost.Geometry bgi::rtree (quadratic, sequential); the repo also benchmarks CPAM and Zd-tree, and has a CGAL kd-tree harness (tests/cgal.cpp)
workload: Real-world point sets GeoLife (3-D), Cosmo50 (3-D) and OSM (2-D): batch build/insert/delete, k-NN (k=1,10,100) and range count/report, parallel PSI trees against a sequential Boost R-tree (script/data/real_world/real_world.csv, from the PPoPP '26 paper's scripts).
claimed_speedup: All ratios derived from page data (real_world.csv, 'tot' column, seconds presumably). Build/insert whole set (ratio 1.0): Cosmo50 Boost 414.38 vs P-Orth (OrthTree) 1.899 and SPaC-Z (PTree-Z) 0.8365 (about 218x and 495x); OSM Boost 666.0 vs OrthTree 4.960 and PTree-Z 2.122 (about 134x and 314x); GeoLife Boost 0.2132 vs OrthTree 0.00639 and PTree-H 0.00150 (about 33x and 142x). Batches of 0.01% of n deleted: Cosmo50 Boost 1482.7 vs OrthTree 17.85 and PTree-Z 8.463 (about 83x and 175x); OSM 264.2 vs 14.93 and 7.368 (about 18x and 36x). Range report (RRL): Cosmo50 Boost 19.25 vs OrthTree 1.738, OSM 8.347 vs 1.128, GeoLife 7.829 vs 0.4466 (about 7-18x). Not uniformly faster: GeoLife batch insert/delete at 0.01% is about equal (Boost 0.0871 vs OrthTree 0.0790), and k=10 in-distribution uniform k-NN is on par for kd/orth trees (Cosmo50 Boost 0.276 vs OrthTree 0.244) and slower for SPaC trees (Cosmo50 PTree-H 1.869, PTree-Z 11.55). Paper (PPoPP '26, per search snippet) says the P-Orth and SPaC trees beat existing parallel kd-trees and orth-trees on batch updates with competitive queries.
compiler_and_flags: Clang >= 19 or g++ >= 14 (CMakeLists check); Release -O3; docs/ARTIFACT_EVALUATION.md says the paper numbers were measured with -march=native -mcx16 (PSI_NATIVE_ARCH=ON). The compiler used for the paper runs is not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated in the repo; artifact doc asks for at least 512 GB RAM and preferably more than 128 cores; run scripts use numactl -i all.
stars_or_usage: 10 stars, 734 commits; PPoPP 2026 (doi 10.1145/3774934.3786412) and SIGMOD 2025 artifacts; successor repo of ucrparlay/Pkd-tree
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 on ParlayLib (submodule) and libmorton; needs many cores to win; points only (2-D to 16-D data generator), kd/orth/SPaC trees chosen per update-heavy vs query-heavy use. SPaC trees are built on a permanent fork of CPAM; vendored Hilbert code carries a Rice University notice requirement (THIRD_PARTY.md). A migration table from bgi::rtree is in docs/MANUAL.md. README notes the code was recently refactored with AI help and gives commit af67b82 for the original design.
caveats: Boost baseline is a single-threaded bgi::rtree, PSI is parallel, so the ratios mostly measure parallelism and batch updates; Boost is competitive or better on small data (GeoLife) and on some k-NN rows. The column meaning of 'tot' is inferred from script/merge_real_world.py. The paper itself (dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu, arXiv 2601.05347) was blocked, so peer review is confirmed only from the README citation and a search snippet; CPU model missing keeps this at B, not A. The other CSVs (summary.csv, knn_3.csv) compare PSI's own trees (solver 'cpam' there is PSI's SPaC build on the CPAM fork, not an external baseline) and contain no CGAL or Zd-tree rows. Fold question: the kd_tree.h tree is the Pkd-tree and the Pkd-tree repo is archived with a pointer to this repo, so Pkd-tree should be treated as a component of PSI-Lib (CGAL and Boost numbers for it are already in the Pkd-tree record); keep this record for P-Orth/SPaC and the Boost R-tree evidence, link both, and prefer this URL as the canonical repo.

name: ikd-Tree (incremental k-d tree)
baseline: PCL static kd-tree (rebuilt per update) and nanoflann kd-tree, plus octree and R*-tree, per the paper
workload: LiDAR-inertial SLAM map maintenance (FAST-LIO2 style): incremental point insertion, box deletion and k-NN on a growing 3-D map.
claimed_speedup: README: ikd-Tree 'incrementally updates a k-d tree with new coming points only, leading to much lower computation time than existing static k-d trees' (no numbers on the page). Paper numbers (arXiv 2102.10808, seen only in WebSearch snippets because arxiv.org is blocked): about 1.6 ms nearly constant update time against more than 10 ms and growing for PCL's static k-d tree on SLAM data; overall about 4% of the computation time of state-of-the-art static implementations; against nanoflann, insertion is often slightly faster for nanoflann but with huge spikes on large maps, while nanoflann's k-NN is slightly slower than ikd-Tree's.
compiler_and_flags: Demo CMakeLists: -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 (links PCL 1.8+); paper flags not seen.
stars_or_usage: 810 stars, 219 forks; used inside FAST-LIO2 (IEEE T-RO 2022)
tradeoffs: GPLv2 (README: contact the authors for commercial use). Dynamic deletion is lazy: points are flagged deleted and removed during a background rebuild, so memory and k-NN cost depend on rebuild timing; threaded rebuild (-pthread). Supports box delete, box/radius search and on-tree downsampling; written for 3-D LiDAR points and later templated (README thanks a contributor for templating it). Demo build requires PCL.
caveats: The repo has a speed demo (examples/ikd_Tree_demo.cpp) that times only ikd-Tree operations; it contains no baseline code, no results and no hardware, so tier C (first-party preprint, unreviewed, could not be opened). FAST-LIO2 (peer-reviewed) uses ikd-Tree but I could not open it. Baselines are not on the category list (PCL kd-tree, nanoflann); the gap against PCL is against a tree that is rebuilt each scan, so it measures incremental vs rebuild. Last commit March 2022; README says GPLv2 without 'or later', so SPDX GPL-2.0-only is an assumption.

name: Kiddo (Rust k-d tree)
baseline: pykdtree, scipy.spatial.KDTree and sklearn KDTree (Python), nabo-rs and FNNTW (Rust); no C++ baseline (nanoflann, PCL, CGAL) is benchmarked
workload: Nearest-1/10/100, within-radius and construction on 100 to 10M random points on a unit sphere, 2-4 dimensions, f32/f64 (companion repo sdd/kd-tree-comparison, Criterion).
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (all-benchmarks.json, 3-D f64, 1,000,000 points, Criterion mean in ns): Query Nearest 1: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 49,798 vs pykdtree 77,187 (about 1.55x), nabo 71,993 (about 1.45x), FNNTW 80,818, scipy 907,836 (about 18x), sklearn 1,911,706 (about 38x). Query Nearest 10: Kiddo_v3_std 109,819 vs pykdtree 199,638 (about 1.8x), scipy 2,227,477 (about 20x). Construction is not faster: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 161.4 ms vs pykdtree 92.3 ms, Kiddo_v3_std 124.6 ms, scipy 294.8 ms.
compiler_and_flags: cargo criterion; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated. The comparison Cargo.toml builds kiddo_v5 with the nightly-only 'simd' feature.
hardware: Ryzen 5900X (12/24 core), 32 GB DDR4 3600 MHz (kd-tree-comparison Readme)
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not callable from C++ without FFI work, so it is outside the C++-first scope and flagged cross-language. Low-dimensional (2-4D) exact and approximate NN; ImmutableKdTree is best for static data, MutableKdTree has no dynamic rebalancing; batch queries multi-threaded by default (rayon); SIMD path needs nightly Rust.
caveats: No numbers against nanoflann or any C++ library exist in the README or the comparison repo (its README says only Rust and Python libraries are tested), so the lead's condition for recording is not met; kept as an out-of-scope flagged record. Author benchmarks his own library (disclosed). Published numbers are for Kiddo v1-v5, while the current release is v6.3.0. The meaning of the Criterion per-iteration unit (the Kiddo bench loops 1,000 query points per iteration) was not reconciled across libraries, so only same-row ratios are quoted. pykdtree is a C extension, the only native-code competitor, and Kiddo beats it on queries but not on construction. The interactive results site (sdd.github.io) is blocked.
